section.title: The Thirty Sayings of the Wise
section.sectionRationale: A new collection begins here, explicitly introduced as 'the words of the wise' in 22:17, distinct from the one-line sentence proverbs of 10:1 to 22:16. Addressed directly to 'my son,' it gathers longer, paragraph-length admonitions traditionally counted as thirty sayings, 22:20, running through 24:22 before a short supplement follows in 24:23-34.
section.thesis: Wisdom is received by incline the ear to the words of the wise, not invented alone, and it shows itself in refusing to exploit the poor, in disciplined appetites and disciplined children, in patience with the wicked's apparent success, and in fearing the LORD and the king rather than joining the rebellious.
section.frameNote: Ten clusters spanning three chapters: the prologue to incline your ear; do not exploit the poor, the angry, or your neighbor; table manners and the futility of chasing riches; instruction, boundaries, and a disciplined son; do not envy sinners or join drunkards; listen to your father, and the deep pit of the adulteress; woe to those who linger over wine; do not envy evil men, for wisdom builds and strengthens; rescue the perishing and taste wisdom's honey; patience with the wicked, and fearing the LORD and the king.

verses.text: Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise, apply your mind to my knowledge,
for it is pleasing when you keep them within you and they are constantly on your lips.
So that your trust may be in the LORD, I instruct you today, yes, you.
Have I not written for you thirty sayings about counsel and knowledge,
to show you true and reliable words, that you may soundly answer those who sent you?

units.label: Do not exploit the poor, the angry, or your neighbor

verses.text: Do not rob a poor man because he is poor, and do not crush the afflicted at the gate,
for the LORD will take up their case and will plunder those who rob them.
Do not make friends with an angry man, and do not associate with a hot-tempered man,
or you may learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.
Do not be one who gives pledges, who puts up security for debts.
If you have nothing with which to pay, why should your bed be taken from under you?
Do not move an ancient boundary stone which your fathers have placed.
Do you see a man skilled in his work? He will be stationed in the presence of kings; he will not stand before obscure men.

units.label: Table manners and the futility of chasing riches

verses.text: When you sit down to dine with a ruler, consider carefully what is set before you,
and put a knife to your throat if you possess a great appetite.
Do not crave his delicacies, for that food is deceptive.
Do not wear yourself out to get rich; be wise enough to restrain yourself.
When you glance at wealth, it disappears, for it makes wings for itself and flies like an eagle to the sky.
Do not eat the bread of a stingy man, and do not crave his delicacies;
for he is keeping track, inwardly counting the cost. "Eat and drink," he says to you, but his heart is not with you.
You will vomit up what little you have eaten and waste your pleasant words.

units.label: Instruction, boundaries, and a disciplined son

verses.text: Do not speak to a fool, for he will despise the wisdom of your words.
Do not move an ancient boundary stone or encroach on the fields of the fatherless,
for their Redeemer is strong; He will take up their case against you.
Apply your heart to {{musar|instruction}} and your ears to words of knowledge.
Do not withhold discipline from a child; although you strike him with a rod, he will not die.
Strike him with a rod, and you will deliver his soul from Sheol.
My son, if your heart is wise, my own heart will indeed rejoice.
My inmost being will rejoice when your lips speak what is right.
Do not let your heart envy sinners, but always continue in the fear of the LORD.
For surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off.
Listen, my son, and be wise, and guide your heart on the right course.
Do not join those who drink too much wine or gorge themselves on meat.
For the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty, and drowsiness will clothe them in rags.
Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old.
Invest in truth and never sell it, in wisdom and instruction and understanding.
The father of a righteous man will greatly rejoice, and he who fathers a wise son will delight in him.
May your father and mother be glad, and may she who gave you birth rejoice!
My son, give me your {{leb|heart}}, and let your eyes delight in my ways.
For a prostitute is a deep pit, and an adulteress is a narrow well.
Like a robber she lies in wait and multiplies the faithless among men.

units.label: Woe to those who linger over wine

verses.text: Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has contentions? Who has complaints? Who has needless wounds? Who has bloodshot eyes?
Those who linger over wine, who go to taste mixed drinks.
Do not gaze at wine while it is red, when it sparkles in the cup and goes down smoothly.
In the end it bites like a snake and stings like a viper.
Your eyes will see strange things, and your mind will utter perversities.
You will be like one sleeping on the high seas or lying on the top of a mast:
"They struck me, but I feel no pain! They beat me, but I did not know it! When can I wake up to search for another drink?"

units.label: Do not envy evil men, for wisdom builds

verses.text: Do not envy wicked men or desire their company;
for their hearts devise violence, and their lips declare trouble.
By {{chokmah|wisdom}} a house is built and by understanding it is established;
through knowledge its rooms are filled with every precious and beautiful treasure.
A wise man is strong, and a man of knowledge enhances his strength.
Only with sound guidance should you wage war, and victory lies in a multitude of counselors.
Wisdom is too high for a fool; he does not open his mouth in the meeting place.
He who plots evil will be called a schemer.
A foolish scheme is sin, and a mocker is detestable to men.

units.label: Rescue the perishing, taste wisdom's honey

verses.text: If you faint in the day of distress, how small is your strength!
Rescue those being led away to death, and restrain those stumbling toward the slaughter.
If you say, "Behold, we did not know about this," does not He who weighs hearts consider it? Does not the One who guards your life know? Will He not repay a man according to his deeds?
Eat honey, my son, for it is good, and the honeycomb is sweet to your taste.
Know therefore that wisdom is sweet to your soul. If you find it, there is a future for you, and your hope will never be cut off.

units.label: Patience with the wicked, fearing the LORD and the king

verses.text: Do not lie in wait, O wicked man, near the dwelling of the righteous; do not destroy his resting place.
For though a righteous man may fall seven times, he still gets up; but the wicked stumble in bad times.
Do not gloat when your enemy falls, and do not let your heart rejoice when he stumbles,
or the LORD will see and disapprove, and turn His wrath away from him.
Do not fret over evildoers, and do not be envious of the wicked.
For the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be extinguished.
My son, fear the LORD and the king, and do not associate with the rebellious.
For they will bring sudden destruction. Who knows what ruin they can bring?

musar.gloss: Instruction, discipline, moral correction. Verse 23:12 calls the son to apply his heart to it, the same word used for the parental discipline of 23:13, showing that both formal teaching and corrective discipline share one Hebrew root: shaping character through received correction, not self-invention.

chokmah.gloss: Wisdom, the skill of ordering life rightly. Verse 24:3 says by wisdom a house is built, a domestic image for how wisdom is not abstract theory but the practical skill that establishes, fills, and sustains a real household, echoing wisdom's larger role in building creation itself, Proverbs 3:19-20.

leb.gloss: Heart, the seat of will, thought, and desire in Hebrew thought, broader than mere emotion. The father's plea in 23:26, 'give me your heart,' asks for the whole inner allegiance of the son, not mere outward compliance, an appeal Scripture applies ultimately to the human heart's response to God.

basic.context: A new section begins here, explicitly called 'the words of the wise,' distinct from the shorter one-line proverbs before it. Addressed directly to 'my son,' it strings together thirty longer admonitions, 22:20, covering everything from not exploiting the poor to refusing envy of the wicked, disciplining children, resisting gluttony and drunkenness, and fearing the LORD and the king rather than joining rebels.
basic.hermeneutics: This is instructional wisdom literature, using direct address and longer paragraphs rather than isolated one-liners, and its commands function as real, binding wisdom for a covenant people even though, like all Proverbs, they describe the normal path of wisdom rather than mechanical guarantees for every case. The famous line, 'have I not written for you thirty sayings,' 22:20, gives this whole unit its name and its scope through 24:22.
basic.originalLanguages: Musar, instruction or discipline, verse 23:12, links formal teaching with the corrective discipline of a child, verse 23:13, one Hebrew root binding both together as parts of the same formative process. Chokmah, wisdom, verse 24:3, is pictured building a literal house, grounding wisdom in practical, domestic skill rather than abstract theory. And leb, heart, verse 23:26, is what the father ultimately asks his son to surrender, the whole inner self, not mere outward behavior.
basic.typology: Wisdom building a house, verse 24:3, anticipates Christ, the wisdom of God through whom all things were made, John 1:3, and who builds His church as a spiritual house on Himself as the cornerstone, 1 Peter 2:4-5. The plea, 'my son, give me your heart,' verse 23:26, anticipates the gospel's call for total allegiance to God, not mere external religion.
basic.christ: This section repeatedly commends wisdom as the builder of a secure house, verse 24:3, a truth fulfilled in Christ, through whom all things were made and who now builds His church as a living house on Himself, John 1:3, 1 Peter 2:4-5. And the father's tender appeal, 'my son, give me your heart,' verse 23:26, anticipates the greater appeal of the gospel, which asks not mere outward conformity but the whole heart's allegiance to God through faith in His Son.
basic.god: God is the defender of the poor and the fatherless, taking up their case Himself, verses 22:23 and 23:11, and He weighs hearts and repays every person according to deeds, verse 24:12, so that no claim of ignorance excuses failing to rescue those in danger. He also disapproves of gloating over a fallen enemy, verse 24:17-18, revealing a character that tempers justice with restraint even toward the wicked.
basic.crossReferences: John 1:3 and 1 Peter 2:4-5 echo wisdom building a house in 24:3. Deuteronomy 19:14 and 27:17 echo the warning against moving ancient boundary stones. Romans 12:19-21 echoes the warning against gloating over a fallen enemy, 24:17. Hebrews 12:5-11 develops the discipline of a son commended in 23:13-14.
basic.oneStory: The thirty sayings call God's people to receive wisdom humbly, refuse to exploit the vulnerable, discipline appetite and children alike, and trust the LORD's justice rather than envying the wicked or gloating over their fall. This whole way of wise living is fulfilled in Christ, the wisdom of God who builds His people into a lasting house and asks for nothing less than the whole heart.

context.literary:
The unit announces its own shape. Verses 22:17 to 21 are a prologue in the style of the opening chapters, with the teacher calling for a listening ear, a mind applied, and a purpose stated outright: 'So that your trust may be in the LORD,' 22:19. Then comes the body, which has a different texture from the one line proverbs of chapters 10 to 22. The sayings run two, three or four verses, open with a prohibition or a conditional ('Do not...', 'When you sit down...'), and give a reason, usually introduced by 'for.' That 'for' is the signature of the section: the teacher does not only forbid, he argues.

The 'thirty' of 22:20 is notoriously hard to count. The BSB footnote notes that the Hebrew word may mean 'excellent sayings' or 'three times,' and different readers divide the text into anywhere from the traditional thirty to a few more or fewer. What matters more than the tally is the movement. The first stretch deals with money and power (22:22 to 23:8): the poor, the debtor, the boundary, the ruler's table, the stingy host. The middle deals with the home and the heart (23:9 to 28): the fool, the fatherless, the disciplined son, the listening father and mother. Then the focus turns to appetite (23:29 to 35) with the famous questions about who has woe, and finally to the company one keeps and the courage to act (24:1 to 22).

Two sayings return like a refrain. The ancient boundary stone is guarded in 22:28 and again in 23:10, and the warning against envying the wicked or sinners appears in 23:17, 24:1 and 24:19. The section also closes on a pairing that frames public life, 'fear the LORD and the king,' 24:21, a loyalty with a clear order of weight.
context.historical:
This block is the one part of Proverbs with a close relative outside Israel. An Egyptian work called the Instruction of Amenemope is organised into thirty short chapters, and a number of its themes and sentences run in parallel with Proverbs 22:17 to 24:22, including the poor man who must not be robbed at the gate, the hot tempered man to avoid, the landmark not to be shifted, and the dangers of a ruler's table. Most scholars think the Hebrew sage knew and reworked the Egyptian material; a minority argue the reverse or a shared source. The date of Amenemope is itself debated, so the direction of borrowing is not settled by the evidence.

What is clear is how Israel handled it. The wise did not copy a foreign creed. They took a widely admired form of court instruction and made it answer to the LORD: the stated aim is trust in Him, 22:19, and the saying about the poor is anchored in His taking up their case, 22:23. This fits what 1 Kings 4:29 to 34 says about the reach of wisdom in Solomon's day, a wisdom that engaged the learning of the nations without surrendering to their gods.

The social world behind the sayings is agrarian and legal. The 'gate' of 22:22 was the open space at a town entrance where elders heard disputes. A 'pledge' or security for a debt, 22:26, could cost a family its bedding, and the law already protected the debtor's cloak, Exodus 22:26 to 27. The boundary stone marked family land held under the covenant, which is why moving it was cursed in Deuteronomy 27:17. A ruler's table, 23:1, is the court dinner where a young official was watched, and the fatherless, 23:10, were the weakest landholders in the village.
context.canonical:
The section draws on the Torah and is drawn on in turn. The protection of the boundary stone repeats Deuteronomy 19:14 and sits under the curse of Deuteronomy 27:17. The conviction that the LORD takes up the cause of the oppressed is the same confidence that stands behind the law of the cloak, Exodus 22:26 to 27, and behind Proverbs 15:25, where He 'protects the boundaries of the widow.' The 'Redeemer' of 23:11 is the go'el, the kinsman who buys back and avenges, the figure of Leviticus 25:25 and Ruth 4, and the one Job names in his hope, Job 19:25. The teacher's claim that God 'weighs hearts,' 24:12, is also made in 21:2 and echoed by Paul when he says God 'will repay each one according to his deeds,' Romans 2:6.

The warning against envying the wicked is a theme the Psalms pick up as a whole lesson: Psalm 37 opens with 'Do not fret because of evildoers,' and Psalm 73 shows the struggle of a believer who nearly slipped looking at the prosperity of the arrogant until he entered God's sanctuary. The advice not to gloat, 24:17, is lived in David's sparing of Saul, 1 Samuel 24:10 to 12, and set in the mouth of Micah, 'Do not gloat over me, my enemy,' Micah 7:8.

The New Testament carries the section into the church. Paul's rule about enemies, Romans 12:17 to 21, follows its logic. The call to 'fear God, honor the king,' 1 Peter 2:17, echoes 24:21. The warning against drink and the promise that discipline is love, Hebrews 12:5 to 6, which quotes Proverbs 3:11 to 12, show how this teaching about the home and the table was received as the voice of the Father.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The teacher meant his son, and the apprentice in the royal service he was training, to hear wisdom as a way of life under the LORD and not as a set of clever tricks for getting on. The prologue says the words are 'pleasing' when they are kept within and 'constantly on your lips,' 22:18, so the aim is formation of the whole person. He wanted the young man to be able to give a 'reliable' answer to whoever sent him, 22:21, which means a person whose speech under pressure could be trusted by employers, judges and neighbours.

The sayings press three convictions. First, power and money are dangerous, and the wise are those who keep their appetite, their pledges and their ambition on a short leash: the knife at the throat of 23:2, the wings that make riches fly off in 23:5. Second, the weak have a Defender who is stronger than they are, so exploiting them is not a safe bet, 22:23, 23:11. Third, there is a future, 23:18, 24:14 and 24:20, and the envy that tempts a young man to join the successful wicked is a failure to see how the story ends. The reader was meant to leave the section more watchful about company, more careful about debt, more patient with appetite, and more convinced that the LORD sees.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This section is full of direct commands, so more of it is prescriptive than a typical page of Proverbs. Do not rob the poor, do not move the boundary, do not rejoice at an enemy's fall: these hold as moral obligations because they rest on the Torah and on the character of God. Other lines are warnings built on observation rather than universal laws. A man skilled in his work being 'stationed in the presence of kings,' 22:29, is how things tend to go, not a promise that every craftsman is promoted, and the deferred hope of 23:18 should be read the same way, as a promise about the end of the story and not the next quarter.

The rod of 23:13 to 14 needs a careful hand. The verses record a parent's duty to correct and give a motive for it; they do not give a licence for harshness, and the same book speaks of the discipline that comes from love, 3:12, and of a father who delights in his child, 23:24. Table manners, such as the knife at the throat in 23:2, are vivid exaggeration (the sage means self control, not self harm). What carries over is the principle, held with the whole of Scripture: restrain appetite, protect the vulnerable, correct with love, and refuse the shortcut that leaves your heart divided.

debates.question: How should Israel's use of the Instruction of Amenemope be understood?

views.label: Israel's sage adapted an Egyptian work
views.case: The similarity in theme and order, together with the number thirty in 22:20, leads many scholars to think the Hebrew teacher knew a form of Amenemope and rewrote it. On this view the LORD is placed where the Egyptian gods stood, and 22:19 states the new purpose.

views.label: Both draw on a common stock of wisdom
views.case: Others argue that the two share a floor of international wisdom about justice, debt and conduct before rulers, so that likeness does not prove dependence. They note that the Hebrew text has its own structure and that the date of Amenemope is itself uncertain.

views.label: Egyptian influence is real but not decisive
views.case: A mediating view grants that the Hebrew author may have used a model, yet points out that every saying has been taken up into a covenant frame, with Torah laws, the LORD's name, and a prologue that places trust in Him first.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is right, nothing in the text suggests the Spirit's work was lessened by the sage's use of what he found. Paul quotes pagan poets in Acts 17:28 without baptising their religion, and the book's own frame says the beginning of knowledge is the fear of the LORD, Proverbs 1:7. The doctrine of inspiration covers what ended up in the text, not how the material was gathered.

debates.question: Does 23:13 to 14 command striking children?

views.label: A plain call to corporal discipline
views.case: The verses speak of a rod and a strike, and 13:24 and 29:15 repeat the idea. Taken at face value they commend measured physical correction as part of parenting, with a motive of love and the child's good, not anger.

views.label: Firm correction in general, using a figure
views.case: The rod in Proverbs is also a shepherd's tool and a symbol of authority, as in Psalm 23:4, so some read the saying as a vivid call to authoritative correction that does not shrink from being unpleasant, not a rule about the method.

views.label: Corporal discipline allowed but limited
views.case: Others argue that the verse permits it while the rest of Scripture sets the limits: fathers are not to provoke their children, Ephesians 6:4, and the goal is to save life, 23:14, not to vent anger.

debates.bearing: All three views agree on the purpose: loving, consistent correction aimed at the child's life, with the father's own delight as the horizon, 23:24 to 25. The verse is never a warrant for cruelty, and Hebrews 12:5 to 6 supplies the pattern of discipline that proves a parent's love.

debates.question: What does it mean that a righteous man 'falls seven times' and gets up, 24:16?

views.label: The righteous suffer misfortune and are restored
views.case: The contrast in the verse is with the wicked who 'stumble in bad times,' so 'fall' most naturally means calamity, as in Micah 7:8 and Psalm 37:24. The righteous are not spared trouble; they are carried through it.

views.label: The righteous sometimes fall into sin and repent
views.case: Many preachers apply the verse to moral failure, with the encouragement that grace restores a believer who repents. The wording does not require this, but it fits the wider biblical picture, 1 John 1:9.

debates.bearing: The first reading is closer to the immediate setting, since the saying warns a wicked man not to plunder the righteous because the righteous will rise. The second is a fair secondary application, so long as it does not excuse the sin or turn the verse into a licence.

study.originalLanguages:
Several of the section's most telling words are hidden in translation. In 23:11 the LORD is the go'el of the fatherless, their 'Redeemer.' The go'el was the kinsman whose duty was to buy back family land, Leviticus 25:25, to redeem a relative sold into debt, Leviticus 25:47 to 49, and to marry the childless widow in the story of Ruth, Ruth 4:1 to 10. The sage says the poorest child in the village has a go'el of unmatched strength. Job uses the same word of his hope, 'my Redeemer lives,' Job 19:25, and Isaiah uses it of the LORD again and again.

In 23:23 the verb behind 'invest' is the ordinary verb for buying, qanah, so the line reads like a market instruction: buy truth, and do not sell it. The verb also stands behind 'get wisdom' in 4:5 and 4:7. The point is that wisdom has a cost and must be held at any price, since the sale of truth for a bribe or a convenience is a bad bargain.

The word acharit, 'future' or 'end,' lies behind the repeated assurance of 23:18, 24:14 and 24:20. It means what comes afterward, the outcome, and it is used of both a person's final end and a hope beyond the present moment. The sage sets this word against envy: the wicked have an 'end' that is cut off, 24:20, and the wise have an 'end' that is not, 23:18. The envy of 23:17 is therefore a failure of arithmetic, because it counts only the present.

The phrase in 23:2, 'if you possess a great appetite,' is literally 'if you are a master of appetite,' with the word nephesh meaning throat or craving, as the footnotes of many translations point out. The sage is not asking for self harm but for the discipline of a man who knows he is dangerously hungry in the presence of someone who is watching him.

The same verb for weighing hearts is found in 24:12 and 21:2, 'the LORD weighs the heart.' It pictures a balance that tests what is inside, not what is displayed. The BSB footnote to 23:7 also warns that the Hebrew of that verse is difficult, and a translator can render it as the host calculating inwardly, or as the man being what he reckons in his soul. The sense for the passage holds either way: a generous looking host with a counting heart is a poor host.

typology.type: The Redeemer of the fatherless, Proverbs 23:11
typology.fulfillment: The go'el who takes up the case of the orphan is the Old Testament pattern of a kinsman who pays what the weak cannot. Christ fulfils it by becoming kin to us: He shared our flesh and blood, Hebrews 2:14, and gave Himself as 'a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. The escalation is that the debt He settles is not a field but a life, and the one He defends is not only the orphan but every sinner. The type falls short in that the earthly go'el could recover land and name; only Christ can bring the dead into an inheritance that does not fade, 1 Peter 1:4.

typology.type: The pledge and the sleeper's bed, Proverbs 22:26 to 27
typology.fulfillment: The sage warns against standing surety because a creditor can take the very bed from under you. The cost of bailing out another is borne by the one who signs. In Christ the warning is turned over: Jesus 'has become the guarantee of a better covenant,' Hebrews 7:22, and willingly stands security for those who cannot pay, taking on the debt and the loss himself. The correspondence is of the shape of the transaction, not of the folly. Where the man of the proverb is rash, Christ's surety is the deliberate act of love, and it cannot fail because He cannot be ruined.

typology.type: The father's rejoicing in a wise son, Proverbs 23:15 to 16 and 23:24 to 25
typology.fulfillment: The longing of a father whose heart rejoices at a son's right words anticipates the Father's voice from heaven at the baptism of Jesus: 'This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,' Matthew 3:17. Luke records that the boy Jesus 'grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man,' Luke 2:52. In Christ the pattern is complete, for He is the Son who never misspeaks, and in Him God's people are made sons who may please the Father. The type falls short in that human fathers rejoice over partial wisdom, while the Father rejoices in a perfect Son and in those united to Him.

typology.type: The house built by wisdom, Proverbs 24:3 to 4
typology.fulfillment: Wisdom builds and fills a house with treasure. Christ is the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:30, the only foundation, 1 Corinthians 3:11, and the builder of a house made of living stones, 1 Peter 2:5. The one who hears His words and does them is like a man who built on the rock, Matthew 7:24. The escalation lies in the materials and the permanence: the proverb's rooms hold goods that can be lost, but His house holds people secured for ever. The picture falls short if it suggests that our wisdom builds the church; the Lord builds the house, Psalm 127:1.

study.christ:
The section leads to Christ along several lines, and the first is the word 'Redeemer.' When the sage says the fatherless have a Redeemer who is strong, 23:11, he uses the vocabulary that Israel would later pour into the hope of salvation. Job's confidence that his Redeemer lives and will stand upon the earth, Job 19:25, looks to a day when the kinsman appears. The New Testament says that day arrived: the Son took on flesh and blood to free those held by fear of death, Hebrews 2:14 to 15, and gave Himself to ransom many, Mark 10:45. The poorest and most exploited person in the proverb has more than a legal protector. He has a kinsman who has already paid.

The second line is the 'discipline that saves.' The father in 23:13 to 14 corrects so that his son is delivered from Sheol. The New Testament reveals the deepest layer of that logic. The prophet says 'the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him,' Isaiah 53:5, and the Hebrew word behind 'punishment' is the same musar that this section uses for instruction and correction. The Son bore the rod that we deserved, so that we are not left to the grave. Hebrews then teaches believers to read their own trials as the discipline of a Father, Hebrews 12:5 to 11, who is not angry but loving.

Third, the section is a portrait of the Wise Son. The father's cry, 'My son, give me your heart,' 23:26, is answered fully only by the Son who gave His entire will to the Father, 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39. He rescued those 'being led away to death,' 24:11, in a literal sense, when He took the place of those condemned, and He cannot be accused of saying 'we did not know,' 24:12, for He knew and came. The saying about gloating, 24:17, finds its answer in the one who prayed for those who crucified Him, Luke 23:34.

The final line is the future. The sage tells the young man 'there is a future for you,' 24:14, against the claims of the envious. In Christ the future is guaranteed by His resurrection, 1 Corinthians 15:20. The righteous man who 'falls seven times' and rises, 24:16, is a picture of His people, never of Him alone; He fell once and rose once and for all. A caution: the sayings are not coded predictions of the Messiah, and the table and the wine are not allegories. The links arise from the New Testament's use of redeemer, discipline and wisdom language.
study.god:
God appears in this section chiefly as a watcher. 'Does not He who weighs hearts consider it?' asks 24:12, and the following questions close every exit: He guards your life, He knows, and He will repay according to deeds. Ignorance is not a refuge when rescue was possible, because the God who weighs the heart knows whether the excuse is honest. The doctrine of divine omniscience is not offered as a puzzle in this passage but as a fact that bears on conduct.

He is also the defender of those without power. The sayings about the poor at the gate and the field of the fatherless do not merely tell the sage to be kind. They announce that God takes up the case Himself, 22:23, and is strong, 23:11. The language is legal: He argues the case, and He takes the plunderer's life for the life that was plundered. Here God's justice is not an abstraction. It has the face of an advocate.

He is concerned with what is inside. The sage notices that the host's mouth and heart disagree, 23:6 to 8, and that the drinker's eyes see 'strange things,' 23:33. The God who weighs hearts is not satisfied with outward manners. In the same way He disapproves of the heart that rejoices at an enemy's fall, 24:17 to 18, even if the enemy deserved it, which shows a justice that guards the mercy He wants us to share, as James 2:13 says, 'Mercy triumphs over judgment.'

He gives a future. The refrain that hope will not be cut off, 23:18 and 24:14, is not a bare optimism. It rests on His faithfulness to those who fear Him. At the same time He lets the lamp of the wicked go out, 24:20. These two sides do not compete; they belong together in a God who keeps the books of history.

He is also the one whose fear anchors every other loyalty. The sage says, 'fear the LORD and the king,' 24:21, in that order, and Peter echoes it, 1 Peter 2:17. Worship, then, is not set aside by civic duty; it orders it. For the reader, this means praying as someone who is seen by a Father who weighs hearts and defends the weak, asking Him to search the heart, Psalm 139:23, and to make us people who rescue and do not gloat, since we are known by the One who does neither lightly.

crossReferences.note: The law of the cloak: a neighbour's garment taken as collateral must be returned by sunset because it is his only covering, and God promises to hear his cry because He is compassionate. This is the legal ground beneath the warning about pledges in 22:26 to 27 and the claim that the LORD takes up the cause of the poor in 22:23.

Moving a neighbour's boundary marker is forbidden because the land was assigned by the LORD. The prohibition lies under the proverb's repeated warning, 22:28 and 23:10, and shows that the sage's economic ethic is simply the covenant applied to daily life.

The psalm's opening command, not to fret over evildoers, shares the sage's lesson in 23:17 and 24:19. The wicked wither like grass, which is the psalm's way of saying what the proverb says with the lamp that goes out: the wicked have no lasting end, so envy misreads the story.

The psalmist nearly slipped because he envied the arrogant when he saw the prosperity of the wicked. His turn, finding the wicked's end in God's sanctuary, is the experience behind the sage's 'there is a future' in 23:18 and 24:14, and it shows how real the temptation to envy was.

The writer quotes Proverbs 3:11 to 12 to teach that the Lord disciplines the one He loves. It frames the rod of 23:13 to 14 as the pattern of the Father's own love, with the aim of life and holiness and with correction that is neither random nor angry.

Paul tells believers not to repay evil for evil and to overcome evil with good. The call to leave vengeance with God, and to meet an enemy's hunger with food, carries on the instruction of 24:17 to 18 and draws from the neighbouring proverb in 25:21 to 22.

Peter's four short commands end with 'fear God, honor the king,' which follows the order of 24:21: God first, the ruler second. It shows that the apostolic teaching on citizenship continues the sage's judgment that loyalty to the king must be held beneath reverence for the LORD.

Paul tells his readers not to be drunk with wine but to be filled with the Spirit. Together with 23:29 to 35, it shows that the issue is not only the damage drink does but the lordship of whatever fills the life, and that the answer is a better filling, not a drier will.

Job's confession, 'I know that my Redeemer lives,' uses the go'el word of 23:11. In the middle of a suffering that looks unjust, Job holds to the kinsman who will take up his case. The sage's promise for the fatherless becomes, in Job, the hope of every sufferer.

Jesus's picture of the wise builder who hears and does His words shows the same wisdom that 'builds a house' in 24:3 to 4, and makes its foundation His own teaching. Storms test the house, and what stands is the life built on what He said.

study.oneStory:
The thirty sayings take up the question left open by the garden: how do people, outside Eden, live together without devouring one another? The story from Genesis 3 onward is one of appetite that grabs, envy that eyes what belongs to someone else, and powerful hands that move the boundary. This section answers with the first lessons of the new life under God: restrain appetite, guard the weak, keep your word, speak the truth, and measure a life by its end and not its moment. In that sense it belongs with the Torah's attempt to teach a redeemed people to live in a fallen world.

It also sets up what follows. The promise of a 'future' that cannot be cut off, 23:18 and 24:14, awaits a king who actually secures it. The Redeemer who is strong, 23:11, awaits the Redeemer of Job, of Isaiah and of Ruth. The father who longs for a wise son's heart, 23:26, awaits a Son who gives it perfectly. Israel's own history shows how hard that was: kings pulled the boundary stones of Naboth's vineyard, 1 Kings 21, nobles crushed the poor at the gate, and the exile followed. The ideal of 22:22 to 23 was not met by the nation, and the gap is a part of the story's pressure toward a better king.

In Christ the pressure resolves. He is the wisdom of God, the Redeemer, the guarantee of a better covenant, and the Son who gave the Father His whole heart. The apostles then speak of discipline, of overcoming evil with good, of honoring the king while fearing God, and of the community as a household built on Him. This is the same wisdom, now carried by the Spirit in the lives of His people.

The story ends where the sage's confidence points. The future that is never cut off is the new creation, where the poor are not robbed at the gate, no boundary stone is moved, and the tree of life bears fruit every month, Revelation 22:2. The lamp of the wicked is out, but the lamp of the city is the Lamb, Revelation 21:23. The young man who was told to keep the fear of the LORD and not envy sinners will find that he was walking toward a city whose Builder is God, Hebrews 11:10.

quiz.q: According to 22:22-23, why should you not rob a poor man?

options.text: Because the LORD will take up their case and plunder those who rob them.
options.note: God Himself defends the poor as their advocate and avenger.

options.text: Because the poor have legal representation available to them.
options.note: The text names the LORD, not human legal systems, as the poor's defender.

options.text: Because it is simply bad for your public reputation.
options.note: The stated reason is the LORD's own defense of the poor, not reputation management.

options.text: Because the poor are usually able to defend themselves.
options.note: This misreads the text, which specifically names the LORD as their defender because they cannot defend themselves at the gate.

quiz.q: What does 23:13-14 counsel about disciplining a child?

options.text: Do not withhold discipline; striking with a rod can deliver his soul from Sheol.
options.note: Timely correction is presented as life-preserving, not merely punitive.

options.text: Discipline should never involve any form of correction.
options.note: This is the opposite of what these verses urge.

options.text: Discipline is only needed for children who are naturally difficult.
options.note: The text gives no such exception; it addresses discipline generally.

options.text: Discipline is helpful but not urgently necessary.
options.note: The verses' urgency, tying discipline to deliverance from Sheol, is stronger than merely 'helpful.'

quiz.q: What warning does 23:31-32 give about wine?

options.text: Do not gaze at it when it sparkles, for in the end it bites like a snake.
options.note: Wine's appeal is deceptive, ending in real harm.

options.text: Wine is harmless as long as it looks appealing.
options.note: This is exactly what the passage warns against trusting.

options.text: Wine should be avoided only in large quantities.
options.note: The warning is about being drawn in by its appeal at all, not merely quantity.

options.text: Wine is dangerous only for those already prone to addiction.
options.note: The text gives a general warning, not one limited to a particular predisposition.

quiz.q: According to 24:11-12, what should you do for those being led away to death, and why?

options.text: Rescue them, since the One who weighs hearts and repays deeds already knows if you claim ignorance.
options.note: God's own knowledge of hearts removes the excuse of claimed ignorance.

options.text: Avoid getting involved to protect your own safety.
options.note: This is the opposite of the command to rescue given here.

options.text: Rescue them only if you personally know them.
options.note: The text gives no such limitation; it is a general call to rescue.

options.text: Report the situation to authorities but take no direct action yourself.
options.note: The text's direct command is to rescue and restrain personally, not merely to report to others.

options.text: Gloating when your enemy falls, since the LORD may disapprove and turn His wrath away from that enemy instead.
options.note: Even justified satisfaction over an enemy's downfall can provoke God's disapproval.

options.text: Ever having enemies at all.
options.note: The passage assumes enemies exist; its concern is the response to their downfall.

options.text: Helping an enemy in any circumstance.
options.note: This is not the warning; the concern is gloating, not helping.

options.text: Feeling any emotion at all when an enemy stumbles.
options.note: The specific warning is against gloating and rejoicing, a stronger and more specific concern than 'any emotion.'

questions: The section opens by calling you to incline your ear to received wisdom, 22:17. What voice of wise counsel have you been resisting or tuning out lately?
Verses 22:22-23 warn against exploiting the poor because the LORD Himself defends them. Who in your circle of influence has less power than you, and how are you treating them?
The wine warning of 23:29-35 pictures a person so numbed they cannot feel the blows landing on them. Is there a habit or substance dulling your ability to feel real consequences in your life?
24:11-12 calls you to rescue those being led toward death, refusing the excuse of claimed ignorance. What need right in front of you have you been pretending not to notice?
24:17-18 warns against gloating over a fallen enemy. Who is someone you have recently seen stumble, and what would it look like to respond with restraint instead of satisfaction?

translationNotes.note: 'Thirty sayings' translates a Hebrew phrase whose consonants can also be read 'excellent things' or 'officers,' but the reading 'thirty' is widely favored since the section that follows can be counted into roughly thirty distinct admonitions.

'For he is keeping track, inwardly counting the cost' renders a difficult Hebrew idiom sometimes translated 'as he calculates within himself,' describing a stingy host who resents every bite his guest takes.

'Though a righteous man may fall seven times, he still gets up' describes repeated setbacks overcome by resilience, not sinless perfection; the number seven functions idiomatically for completeness or repetition.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched via the Makor scripture toolkit for Proverbs 22:17-24:22, spanning three chapters.
